meta.title: Human memory datasets: one catalogue for a unified trial-level model of memory behaviour

task.recognition: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)
task.recall: Recall (produce the item; nothing is shown)
task.reproduction: Reproduction / continuous report (reproduce a feature value such as a colour angle; also called delayed estimation or continuous recall)

metric.trial_sequence: Per-trial sequence (which item next, in order)
metric.aggregate: Aggregate score (memorability score, hit / false-alarm rate)

notes: Each dataset is placed on three axes: how long the memory is held, what the task asks, and what kind of measurement is released.

The metric shown for each dataset is the one its own literature uses; the strongest released models are listed on that metric, followed by our unified model (one model for every dataset, no dataset-specific parameters, 6000 training steps). Cells are left blank when a number was not measured.
Published numbers were verified at source; figures are clipped from the original papers or author manuscripts for academic summary and carry their source and licence.

datasets.name: LaMem
datasets.task_text: A memory game: a stream of natural images, one every 1.4 s; press a key when an image repeats. Only the per-image memorability score is released.
datasets.response: key press on repeats, summarised as one score per image
datasets.metric_name: Spearman rank correlation with human memorability
datasets.metric_intuition: How well the ranking of images by predicted memorability agrees with the ranking by measured hit rate (1 = identical order, 0 = unrelated).
datasets.metric_formula: rho = Pearson correlation between the ranks of predicted and measured scores over the test images; mean over the five official 45k/4k/10k splits.

rows.note: protocol simulation of the memory game; the model never saw LaMem trials

datasets.task_label: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)
datasets.metric_label: Aggregate score (memorability score, hit / false-alarm rate)

datasets.name: MemCat
datasets.task_text: Repeat-detection memory game on 10,000 category-labelled images; press when an image repeats. Every key press of 2,291 participants is released.
datasets.metric_name: Spearman rank correlation with measured memorability
datasets.metric_intuition: Whether the images the model expects to be remembered are the ones people actually remembered.
datasets.metric_formula: rho between the model's mean predicted hit probability per image and the observed hit rate per image (our held-out images with at least 20 repeat trials).

rows.method: MemNet, off the shelf (reported in the MemCat paper)

rows.note: split unspecified; above the raw human ceiling

datasets.name: THINGS memorability
datasets.task_text: Online continuous recognition over 26,107 object images; press when an image repeats. The released quantity is the corrected recognition score per image; raw trials were not released.
datasets.paper: Kramer, Hebart, Baker & Bainbridge, Science Advances 2023
datasets.metric_name: Spearman rank correlation with corrected recognition
datasets.metric_intuition: Agreement between the model's ranking of objects and people's, where an object's score is how often it was recognised minus how often it was falsely recognised.
datasets.metric_formula: CR = hit rate minus false-alarm rate per image; rho = rank correlation between predicted and measured CR over held-out images.

rows.note: zero-shot: never trained on THINGS; protocol simulation

datasets.task_label: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)
datasets.metric_label: Aggregate score (memorability score, hit / false-alarm rate)

figure.title: The features underlying the memorability of objects

datasets.name: NSD
datasets.full: Natural Scenes Dataset, continuous recognition task
datasets.task_text: Eight people each saw about 10,000 photographs three times over 30 to 40 sessions spanning up to a year, and on every trial reported whether the image had been seen before at any point in the experiment.
datasets.metric_intuition: How well a participant separates old from new images, independent of their bias to say 'old'.
datasets.metric_formula: d' = z(hit rate) minus z(false-alarm rate), z = inverse normal; computed per participant from old/new responses and averaged.
datasets.task_label: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)

datasets.name: CNeuroMod-THINGS
datasets.task_text: Four people viewed THINGS images across many sessions and answered with four keys: sure seen, maybe seen, maybe unseen, sure unseen.
datasets.metric_intuition: How well the participant separates seen from unseen images once the four keys are collapsed to seen / unseen.
datasets.metric_formula: d' = z(hit rate) minus z(false-alarm rate) after collapsing 'sure seen' + 'maybe seen' to 'seen'; per participant, then averaged.

rows.dprime: human 1.54 to 1.90 per participant (St-Laurent et al.)

datasets.task_label: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)

datasets.name: MST
datasets.task_text: Study a list of objects; at test each item is a repeat (target), a similar-looking new object (lure) or a new object (foil); answer old, similar or new.
datasets.stimuli: object photographs with lures in five similarity bins
datasets.paper: Stark, Kirwan & Stark, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 2019
datasets.metric_name: Lure discrimination index (LDI) and recognition score (REC)
datasets.metric_intuition: LDI: how much more often people call a similar lure 'similar' than a brand-new foil; REC: how much more often a repeat is called 'old' than a foil.
datasets.metric_formula: LDI = p(similar | lure) minus p(similar | foil); REC = p(old | target) minus p(old | foil); per participant, then averaged.

rows.note: fit the condition labels only; no predictive number published

datasets.ceiling: LDI test-retest 0.69 to 0.75 within a session
datasets.task_label: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)

datasets.name: PEERS recognition
datasets.task_text: After the free-recall lists of a session, participants judged studied and unstudied words as old or new with a confidence rating.
datasets.metric_intuition: How well the participant separates studied from unstudied words.
datasets.metric_formula: d' = z(hit rate) minus z(false-alarm rate) after collapsing the confidence scale to old / new; per participant, then averaged.
datasets.task_label: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)

figure.caption_short: The end-of-session recognition path in PEERS: after studying 16 lists of 16 words and doing immediate free recall, subjects take an item-recognition test with confidence judgements (and, in half the sessions, a 5-minute final free-recall test first).
figure.license: author manuscript, PMC (NIHMS-2084225); published version copyright American Psychological Association - figure reproduced under fair use for academic summary

datasets.name: PEERS free recall
datasets.full: Penn Electrophysiology of Encoding and Retrieval Study, immediate free recall
datasets.task_text: Lists of 16 words shown one at a time, then recall as many as possible in any order. Every recall event in output order is kept, including intrusions.
datasets.response: spoken sequence of words, then stop
datasets.metric_name: Recall curves: probability of first recall and lag-CRP
datasets.metric_intuition: Whether the model recalls from the same list positions people start from, and whether it moves to neighbouring items the way people do.
datasets.metric_formula: PFR(i) = fraction of lists whose first recall was list position i; lag-CRP(k) = probability that the next recall is k positions away from the last one, over available transitions. We report the correlation between the model's and the participants' curves.

rows.nll: 2.98 (held-out; candidates = every word in memory + stop + other)

datasets.task_label: Recall (produce the item; nothing is shown)
datasets.metric_label: Per-trial sequence (which item next, in order)

datasets.name: MaiMemo
datasets.task_text: Review logs of a vocabulary app: for each learner and word, the times of each review and whether the word was recalled.
datasets.paper: Ye, Su & Cao, KDD 2022 (dataset); Su et al. 2023
datasets.metric_name: Mean absolute error of predicted recall probability
datasets.metric_intuition: On average, how far the predicted chance of recalling a word is from the recall rate actually observed for reviews with the same history.
datasets.metric_formula: MAE = mean over review-history groups of |mean predicted p minus observed recall rate|, weighted by group size (groups defined by number of earlier reviews, interval since the last review and its outcome).

rows.note: MAE not comparable: the paper's review-history groups cannot be rebuilt from raw logs; our per-review AUC is given instead

datasets.name: Digit span (TestMyBrain)
datasets.task_text: Digits appear one at a time; type them back in the same order (forward) or reversed (backward); lists get longer after each correct answer.

figure.venue: Journal of Clinical and Experimental Neuropsychology 43(8):786-795

FALLBACK SOURCE, two levels down. (1) The paper named first in the brief - Hartshorne & Germine 2015, 'When does cognitive functioning peak?', Psychological Science 26(4):433-443, PMC4441622 - contains NO paradigm figure. Verified against the PMC XML and the downloaded author manuscript (site/papers/hartshorne2015.pdf): all four of its figures are results plots (bootstrapped ages of peak performance, lifespan curves, cross-experiment replications, vocabulary cohort curves). (2) This TestMyBrain toolkit paper (the 'Singh, Germine et al. 2021 JCEN 43:786' fallback in the brief) was used instead. Its Figure 1 ('Visualization of tests included in the DNT') is a schematic icon board of the whole battery; the crop is the Working Memory group, which is the only digit-span-specific graphic in either paper. Caveat: it is an illustrative stimulus icon, not a live task screen - it does not show the digits appearing one at a time, the response box, or the adaptive length staircase; the paper's Methods text supplies those details. (3) A screenshot of the live TestMyBrain digit-span demo was deliberately NOT taken: the public entry points (v3.testmybrain.org/cogsci, v3.testmybrain.org/digitallab) launch active data-collecting research studies, and the static pages (cogsci.testmybrain.org test list) carry only prose descriptions, no task screenshots. Extracted from the figure's embedded 1800x864 300-dpi JPEG (pdfimages confirms page 12 carries exactly this asset), cropped to the Working Memory group (442x410 px at source scale) and upsampled 2x with Lanczos to 884x820 for legibility on the site; no other processing.

datasets.name: 2AFC objects
datasets.full: Spatial two-alternative forced-choice recognition of real-world objects
datasets.task_text: Six object photographs are shown together for 2 s; after a short delay two objects appear at one location, the studied one and a foil of graded similarity, and the participant picks the studied one.

datasets.metric_intuition: How often the studied object is chosen over the foil.
datasets.metric_formula: percent correct = 100 x (number of trials where the studied object was chosen) / (number of trials); the model's value is its mean predicted probability of the correct choice.

figure.title: Comparing memory capacity across stimuli requires maximally dissimilar foils: Using deep convolutional neural networks to understand visual working memory capacity for real-world objects
figure.authors: Timothy F. Brady, Viola S. Störmer
figure.caption_short: Method of Experiment 2: participants saw six real-world objects for 2000 ms, held them over a 700 ms delay, and then made a two-alternative forced choice at a cued location between the studied object and a foil.
figure.license: publisher copyright (© The Psychonomic Society, Inc. 2023; Springer Nature holds exclusive rights under a publishing agreement) — author self-archived PDF of the published version from the Brady lab website; used under fair use for academic summary
figure.notes: Cropped from page 8 (journal page 602) of the published typeset PDF at 440 dpi; caption text excluded. Fig. 4 shows the full trial: 6-object memory array (2000 ms, spatial placeholders visible throughout) -> 700 ms delay -> 2-AFC test at one cued location with the studied object and one foil. The foil-similarity manipulation is described in the caption rather than drawn as separate panels: foils were maximally distinct cross-category, minimally distinct cross-category, or randomly chosen from a different category (60 trials each, 180 total, N = 50 MTurk participants). The example pairs for the similarity conditions are shown separately in Fig. 2, and the CNN foil-selection method in Fig. 1. Fig. 6 (page 10) is the analogous method figure for Experiment 3, which contrasts objects with colors. Not open access: Crossref registers only a Springer Nature text-and-data-mining license (no CC license), and no PMC record was found. The OSF node https://osf.io/axyqs/ is a public project holding materials, data and analysis code — the OSF preprints API returns 404 for that identifier, so it is not a preprint. The author self-archived copy at bradylab.ucsd.edu was therefore used.

datasets.name: Colour delayed estimation
datasets.full: van den Berg, Awh & Ma delayed-estimation benchmark (colour)
datasets.task_text: One to eight coloured items are shown briefly; after a delay one location is cued and the participant reproduces its colour on a colour wheel.
datasets.paper: van den Berg, Awh & Ma, Psychological Review 2014
datasets.metric_name: Per-trial likelihood of the reported colour
datasets.metric_intuition: How much probability the model puts on the colour the participant actually reported; the benchmark ranks models by this likelihood (as AIC) per participant.
datasets.metric_formula: NLL = minus the mean log density of the reported angle under the model's predicted circular distribution (nats; the uniform distribution scores 1.84). AIC = 2k minus 2 log-likelihood; lower is better.

columns.label: error SD by set size (observed / decoded)

rows.note: best model by AIC in 79% of the 164 participants; per-trial numbers not published

rows.method: mixture model fitted per set size (our reference)

datasets.task_label: Reproduction / continuous report (reproduce a feature value such as a colour angle; also called delayed estimation or continuous recall)

figure.title: Factorial Comparison of Working Memory Models
figure.authors: Ronald van den Berg, Edward Awh, Wei Ji Ma
figure.caption_short: Example trial procedure in delayed estimation of color: subjects view a set of colored items, and after a brief delay report the color of one probed item by clicking on a color wheel.
figure.license: publisher copyright (© 2014 American Psychological Association) — author self-archived copy of the published version from the Ma lab website (cns.nyu.edu/malab); used under fair use for academic summary
figure.notes: Cropped from page 3 (journal page 126) of the published APA typeset PDF at 440 dpi; caption text excluded. Figure 2 is the paper's schematic of the delayed-estimation paradigm (memory array -> delay -> continuous report on a color wheel). The delayed-estimation benchmark analysed in this paper pools 10 previously published experiments (Table 1, same page): E1 Wilken & Ma 2004 (color wheel, Caltech); E2 Zhang & Luck 2008 (color wheel, UC Davis); E3 Bays et al. 2009 (color wheel, UCL); E4 Anderson et al. 2011 (orientation 360deg, U Oregon); E5 Anderson & Awh 2012 (orientation 180deg, U Oregon); E6 Anderson & Awh 2012 (orientation 360deg, U Oregon); E7-E9 Van den Berg et al. 2012 (color scrolling, color wheel, orientation 180deg; Baylor); E10 Rademaker et al. 2012 (orientation 180deg, Vanderbilt). Combined: 164 subjects, 131,452 trials. Figure 2 illustrates the color-wheel version; orientation experiments used an analogous continuous report. Data and code: https://github.com/WeiJiMaLab/delayed_estimation_benchmark. The PMC author-manuscript version is PMC4159389 (its PDF is behind a proof-of-work challenge; the Ma lab copy was used instead — note the task brief cited PMC3949221, but Unpaywall/PMC resolve DOI 10.1037/a0035234 to PMC4159389).

datasets.name: Change detection
datasets.full: Keshvari, van den Berg & Ma change detection (colour and orientation)
datasets.task_text: A display of two to eight items is shown, then after a delay a second display in which one item may have changed by a graded amount; answer same or different.
datasets.paper: Keshvari, van den Berg & Ma, PLoS Computational Biology 2013
datasets.metric_intuition: How often the change judgement is right, and how many items that accuracy implies were held in memory.
datasets.metric_formula: K = N x (hit rate minus false-alarm rate) / (1 minus false-alarm rate) for a display of N items (whole-display formula); the model's value uses its predicted 'different' responses.

rows.note: ranked by log marginal likelihood against slot models; per-trial numbers not published

datasets.task_label: Recognition (a probe is shown; judge whether it is in memory)

figure.title: No Evidence for an Item Limit in Change Detection
figure.authors: Shaiyan Keshvari, Ronald van den Berg, Wei Ji Ma
figure.caption_short: Orientation change detection trial sequence: a first display of oriented ellipses (100 ms), a 1000 ms delay, a second display (100 ms), and an unspeeded same/different ("change") response.
figure.license: CC BY 4.0 (PLOS gold open access; Crossref registers http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ — the article text itself says "Creative Commons Attribution License" without a version number)
figure.notes: Cropped panel (a) only of Figure 2 from page 4 at 440 dpi; panel label 'a' retained, panels (b) hit/false-alarm rates and (c) psychometric curves and the caption excluded, since only panel (a) shows the paradigm. The paper reports two change-detection experiments (orientation and color) in which change magnitude was drawn from a wide range including small changes; Figure 2a depicts the orientation version, and the color experiment used the same trial structure with colored disks. Set sizes were N = 2, 4, 6, 8.
